title: 0/1 Knapsack Problem
description: Learn how Dynamic Programming solves constrained optimization problems by maximizing value while respecting limited capacity constraints.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The 0/1 Knapsack Problem is one of the most famous applications of Dynamic Programming.

The problem focuses on optimal selection under constraints.

Suppose a bag has a limited carrying capacity. We are given several items, each with a weight and a value.

The objective is to maximize total value without exceeding the bag's capacity.

Each item can only be selected once, which is why the problem is called 0/1 Knapsack.

sections.title: Why the Knapsack Problem Matters
sections.content:
Many real-world systems involve limited resources and optimization constraints.

Examples include investment planning, cargo loading, budget optimization, server resource allocation, and project selection.

The challenge is maximizing benefit while respecting capacity limitations.

The Knapsack Problem models this optimization challenge computationally.
bullets: Appears in many real-world optimization systems.

sections.title: Problem Setup
sections.content:
Suppose we have the following items:

Item A → Weight = 1, Value = 15
Item B → Weight = 3, Value = 20
Item C → Weight = 4, Value = 30

Knapsack capacity:
4

The objective is to maximize total value without exceeding the weight limit.

sections.title: Why Greedy Selection Fails
sections.content:
A common beginner instinct is selecting the item with the highest value first.

Suppose we choose item C with value 30.

Although this seems attractive locally, selecting items A and B together produces total value 35, which is better.

This demonstrates that local greedy decisions may fail globally.

Dynamic Programming solves this by efficiently exploring multiple combinations.

sections.title: Core Dynamic Programming Idea
sections.content:
Dynamic Programming solves Knapsack by storing solutions to smaller capacity problems.

Instead of repeatedly recalculating combinations, the algorithm remembers previously computed optimal values.

This allows larger optimal solutions to be built from smaller optimal subproblems.

sections.title: Understanding the DP Matrix
sections.content:
The most important structure in Knapsack Dynamic Programming is the 2D matrix.

Rows represent items considered.

Columns represent available knapsack capacities.

Each matrix cell stores the maximum achievable value for that specific subproblem.

The matrix gradually fills row by row and capacity by capacity.

sections.title: DP Matrix Visualization
sections.content:
Suppose the capacity is 4.

The DP table gradually fills using previous optimal values.

Each row introduces a new item, while each column represents increasing capacity.

This transforms recursive optimization into structured table-based computation.

sections.title: Decision-Making Per DP Cell
sections.content:
At every matrix cell, the algorithm decides whether to include or exclude the current item.

Option 1 — Exclude the item:
Keep the previous best value.

Option 2 — Include the item:
Add the current item value plus the best value from the remaining capacity.

The algorithm selects the larger result between these two choices.

sections.title: Knapsack Recurrence Relation
sections.content:
The mathematical core of Knapsack Dynamic Programming becomes:

dp[i][w] = max(
    dp[i-1][w],
    value[i] + dp[i-1][w-weight[i]]
)

This recurrence drives the optimization process by comparing inclusion and exclusion choices.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Suppose the capacity is 4.

First, process item A with weight 1 and value 15.

Next, process item B with weight 3 and value 20.

At capacity 4, the algorithm compares:

Exclude B → value 15
Include B → 20 + 15 = 35

The algorithm chooses 35.

Finally, processing item C shows that value 35 remains optimal.

The final solution becomes selecting items A and B.

sections.title: Knapsack Pseudocode Pattern
sections.content:
The algorithm processes every item and every capacity.

If the item weight fits within the current capacity, the algorithm compares inclusion and exclusion results.

Otherwise, the previous best value is copied.

This repeated matrix transition is the heart of Knapsack Dynamic Programming.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: Knapsack implementations commonly use a 2D Dynamic Programming matrix to store optimal intermediate results.

codeSnippets.title: 0/1 Knapsack implementation
codeSnippets.code:
weights = [1, 3, 4]
values = [15, 20, 30]
capacity = 4
n = len(weights)

dp = [[0 for _ in range(capacity + 1)]
for _ in range(n + 1)]

for i in range(1, n + 1):
    for w in range(capacity + 1):
        if weights[i - 1] <= w:
            include = values[i - 1] + \
            dp[i - 1][w - weights[i - 1]]

            exclude = dp[i - 1][w]

            dp[i][w] = max(include, exclude)
        else:
            dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w]

print(dp[n][capacity])

codeSnippets.title: Create an empty DP matrix
codeSnippets.code:
rows = 4
cols = 5

dp = [[0 for _ in range(cols)]
for _ in range(rows)]

for row in dp:
    print(row)

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
The algorithm fills every DP matrix cell once.

If there are n items and capacity W, the matrix contains n × W subproblems.

This produces O(n × W) time complexity and O(n × W) space complexity.

Dynamic Programming transforms exponential brute-force combinations into scalable polynomial-time optimization.

chart.description: Dynamic Programming transforms exponential recursive combination search into structured polynomial-time optimization.

sections.title: Why Knapsack Uses Dynamic Programming
sections.content:
The Knapsack Problem contains overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.

Without Dynamic Programming, recursive combinations become exponentially expensive.

DP avoids repeated computation by storing optimal intermediate results.

This transforms impractical brute-force search into efficient optimization.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Knapsack optimization appears in cargo loading, investment planning, cloud resource allocation, portfolio management, manufacturing systems, advertisement selection, and budget optimization.

Many business optimization systems use knapsack-style decision modeling.

subsections.title: Mistake: Using greedy selection for 0/1 Knapsack
subsections.content: Greedy selection does not always produce optimal answers for 0/1 Knapsack.

subsections.title: Mistake: Confusing 0/1 Knapsack with Fractional Knapsack
subsections.content: 0/1 Knapsack only allows complete selection or rejection of items, while Fractional Knapsack allows partial selection.

subsections.title: Mistake: Misunderstanding DP matrix meaning
subsections.content: Each DP cell represents the best achievable value for a specific subproblem.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: The 0/1 Knapsack Problem focuses on optimal selection under constraints.
Each item can either be selected or skipped.
Greedy selection does not always work correctly.
Dynamic Programming stores optimal subproblem solutions.
The DP matrix represents capacities and item decisions.
Knapsack optimization demonstrates powerful DP reasoning.
